title: Catastrophizing About Job Interview
situation: Priya, a 26-year-old job seeker, has an important interview tomorrow and is catastrophizing about the outcome. She believes one bad interview will ruin her entire career.
user_turns: I have a big interview tomorrow and I'm convinced I'm going to fail it. If I mess this up, my career is over. I always freeze under pressure.
I've failed two interviews before. That proves I'm just not good enough for this kind of role. I don't know why I even bother applying.
Even if I prepare, something will go wrong. I'll blank on a question or say something stupid. I can't control it.
What if I try to challenge that thought and it doesn't work? What if the negative thought is actually true?

title: All-or-Nothing Thinking in Relationships
situation: James, a 30-year-old, ended a long-term relationship and now believes he is fundamentally unlovable and will never find a healthy relationship.
user_turns: My relationship ended after three years. I've decided I'm just not someone who can maintain a healthy relationship. I'm fundamentally broken.
Every relationship I've had has ended. That's not a coincidence — it's a pattern that proves something is wrong with me.
I know I should think differently but the evidence keeps pointing to the same conclusion. How do I challenge a thought that feels completely true?
What would a thought record even look like for something like this? I've never done one before.

title: Mind Reading at Work
situation: Sophie, a 28-year-old, is convinced her manager dislikes her based on minimal evidence — a brief email response and being left off a meeting invite. She is spiraling into anxiety about her job security.
user_turns: My manager sent me a really short reply to my email today and didn't invite me to a team meeting. I'm sure she hates me and is planning to fire me.
I keep replaying her tone in my head. She definitely seemed cold. I can just tell when someone doesn't like me.
I've been anxious about this all day. I can't focus on my work because I keep imagining the worst-case scenario.
How do I stop my brain from jumping to conclusions? It happens automatically and I can't seem to control it.

title: Should Statements and Guilt
situation: Marcus, a 33-year-old father, feels intense guilt for taking time for himself. He believes he should always be available for his children and that wanting personal time makes him a bad parent.
user_turns: I went to the gym yesterday while my wife watched the kids and I felt guilty the entire time. I should always be there for my children. Taking time for myself is selfish.
I know logically that parents need breaks but emotionally I can't shake the feeling that I'm failing them when I'm not present.
My own father was always there. He never took time for himself. I feel like I'm not living up to that standard.
What's the difference between a healthy standard and an unrealistic one? How do I know which one I'm dealing with?

title: Overgeneralization After Social Rejection
situation: Lily, a 22-year-old, was not invited to a friend group outing and has generalized this to mean that nobody likes her and she will always be excluded.
user_turns: My friends went out without inviting me last weekend. This always happens to me. Nobody actually likes me — they just tolerate me.
I've been excluded before. It's a pattern. I'm always the one left out. I must be doing something wrong that pushes people away.
Even when I'm included, I feel like I'm only there because they felt obligated. I can't trust that anyone genuinely wants me around.
I've tried telling myself it's not true but the feeling doesn't go away. What am I supposed to do when the thought keeps coming back?

title: Cognitive Distortions Around Health Anxiety
situation: Tom, a 40-year-old, has been experiencing health anxiety after reading about a serious illness online. He is convinced he has the disease despite no medical diagnosis.
user_turns: I've been having headaches for a week and I looked it up online. I'm convinced I have a brain tumor. The symptoms match perfectly.
I know doctors say it's probably nothing but they could be wrong. I can't stop thinking about it. I've checked my symptoms ten times today.
Every time I try to distract myself, the thought comes back. What if I'm one of those people who gets dismissed and it turns out to be serious?
How do I challenge a thought when there's a small chance it could actually be true? I don't want to dismiss something real.

title: Negative Core Belief - Worthlessness
situation: Nina, a 31-year-old, has a deep-seated core belief that she is worthless, stemming from childhood criticism. This belief filters how she interprets all life events.
user_turns: I've always believed I'm worthless. It's not just a thought — it feels like a fact about who I am. Everything that goes wrong confirms it.
When something good happens, I dismiss it as luck. When something bad happens, it proves I'm worthless. I can't seem to update this belief.
My therapist mentioned core beliefs but I don't understand how to change something that feels so fundamental to who I am.
What does it even look like to challenge a belief you've held your whole life? Where do you even start?
